newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania pursues budget debate to win over IMF.
newsitem.headline: Romania pursues budget debate to win over IMF.

text.p: Romania's centrist government pulled back from a deal to build nearly 100 combat helicopters with a U.S. firm on Tuesday as part of its effort to revise the 1997 budget to win IMF approval for fresh credits.

But tortuous negotiations were continuing on individual ministries' allocations in a bid to agree the new budget the International Monetary Fund has insisted on as a condition for the release of the second of five $86 million credits.
The government is committed to drawing up new spending limits to keep the deficit to within the IMF goal of 4.5 percent of gross domestic product despite higher inflation.

However, there were new pressures on the budget from trade unions, who claimed victory in pay negotiations with Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea, and from flooding which threatened an expected bumper grain harvest and destroyed a njumber of homes.

Few details have emerged of the government's plans to revise the budget. The IMF was expected to say on Wednesday whether it backed the new budget, and to pass judgement on Bucharest's progress in curbing inflation, proceeding with stalled privatisation and closing down inefficient farms and companies.
Finance Minister Mircea Ciumara said the government would not back a deal this year to co-produce 96 Cobra attack helicopters with the U.S. firm Bell Helicopter Textron.
"The state will not guarantee the deal with Bell Helicopters in 1997," he told Reuters, making no mention of any new deadline.

The $2 billion deal would be the biggest project in post-communist Romania. It is part of the country's efforts to align its military equipment to NATO standards, with an eye to an securing eventual membership of the Alliance after being refused entry in the first wave last month.

Media reports earlier in the day said the IMF had opposed demands by the government to extend by $2 billion the ceiling of its external borrowings -- a measure which would have included the funds for the Cobra deal. Neither the government nor IMF officials commented on the reports.

But trade union negotiators said they had won a 17 percent wage indexation for the third quarter of 1997 and six percent for the fourth quarter, as well as a promise to continue subsidised electricity prices through next winter.

"This indexation should be combined with tax cuts and should lead to an increase in real wages of 16 percent until the end of the year," Dumitru Costin, leader of the National Trade Union (BNSD) bloc, told reporters.
No government minister was available to comment on the outcome of the talks, broken off last week when the unions walked out and accused ministers of botching reforms.

Since the centrists defeated ex-communists in last year's election, they have pledged to make up for seven years of stalling which left Romania's economic reforms trailing far behind those of Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.

Monthly inflation, which soared to more than 30 percent in March after price liberalisation, is expected to fall below two percent this month, but the government's original target of 90 percent for the year has long since passed out of reach.
Nevertheless, ministers have pledged to stick to their original target of reducing the budget deficit to 4.5 percent of Gross Domestic Product from last year's 5.8 percent.
But there was bad news as heavy rains put tens of thousands of hectares (acres) of farmland under water, threatening a forecast bumper grain crop and destroying hundreds of homes.
Two people were killed, bringing to eight the death toll in two weeks of flooding. The government said it would ask the United States and European Union for emergency aid.
